items.followUp: Define diffusion and give one example.

rubric.why: Shows the defining feature of effusion.
rubric.description: States that effusion is the escape of gas molecules through a tiny hole into a vacuum.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for identifying both the tiny opening and the vacuum (or low-pressure space).

rubric.why: A relevant example demonstrates the process.
rubric.description: Gives a suitable example of a gas escaping through a small opening.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for an example that clearly involves gas passing through a small opening.

modelAnswer: Effusion is the escape of gas molecules through a tiny hole into a vacuum or a region of lower pressure.
For example, helium gas escapes through tiny pores in a balloon.

items.followUp: Define viscosity and give one example of a highly viscous liquid.

rubric.why: Identifies malleability as the ability to be shaped by hammering.
rubric.description: Defines malleable as the ability of a substance to be hammered or rolled into thin sheets.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the correct meaning of malleable.

rubric.why: Identifies ductility as the ability to be drawn into wire.
rubric.description: Defines ductile as the ability of a substance to be drawn into thin wires.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the correct meaning of ductile.

modelAnswer: A malleable substance can be hammered or rolled into thin sheets.
A ductile substance can be drawn into thin wires.

items.followUp: Define an atom and classify molecules according to the number of atoms they contain.

rubric.why: A molecule is defined by its independent existence and retention of chemical properties.
rubric.description: Defines a molecule as the smallest particle of a substance that can exist independently and retain its chemical properties.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for a substantially correct definition.

rubric.why: Identifies molecules containing one atom and gives a suitable example or description.
rubric.description: Describes monoatomic molecules as containing one atom, with a suitable example.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the monoatomic type and its description or example.

rubric.why: Identifies molecules containing two atoms and gives a suitable example or description.
rubric.description: Describes diatomic molecules as containing two atoms, with a suitable example.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the diatomic type and its description or example.

rubric.why: Recognizes molecules containing three atoms and those containing more than three atoms.
rubric.description: Describes triatomic and polyatomic molecules, with their atom counts or suitable examples.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for correctly describing both types.

modelAnswer: A molecule is the smallest particle of a substance that can exist independently and retain its chemical properties.
A monoatomic molecule contains one atom; for example, helium (He).
A diatomic molecule contains two atoms; for example, hydrogen (H₂).
A triatomic molecule contains three atoms; for example, water (H₂O).
A polyatomic molecule contains more than three atoms; for example, phosphorus (P₄).

items.followUp: Write four postulates of Dalton’s atomic theory.

rubric.why: Describes electrons occupying definite orbits or energy levels around the nucleus.
rubric.description: States that electrons revolve around the nucleus in fixed orbits or energy levels.
rubric.how: Award 2 marks for this postulate.

rubric.why: States the stability of electrons in allowed stationary orbits.
rubric.description: States that electrons do not radiate energy while remaining in a stationary orbit.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for this postulate.

rubric.why: Explains that energy changes occur when electrons move between energy levels.
rubric.description: States that an electron absorbs or emits a definite amount of energy when it jumps between orbits.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for this postulate.

rubric.why: Gives another fundamental feature of Bohr’s model.
rubric.description: States that electron angular momentum is quantized or that electron energies have definite discrete values.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for this additional postulate.

modelAnswer: Electrons revolve around the nucleus in certain fixed orbits or energy levels.
Electrons do not radiate energy while moving in a stationary orbit.
An electron absorbs energy to move to a higher orbit and emits energy when it moves to a lower orbit.
The energy of an electron in an allowed orbit has a definite value; the energy levels are discrete.
The angular momentum of an electron in an allowed orbit is quantized.

items.followUp: What is a covalent compound? State four of its properties.

rubric.why: High melting and boiling points are characteristic properties of ionic compounds.
rubric.description: States that ionic compounds generally have high melting and boiling points.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for this property.

rubric.why: Ionic compounds commonly form hard crystalline solids.
rubric.description: States that ionic compounds are hard crystalline solids.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for this property.

rubric.why: Many ionic compounds dissolve in water, a standard textbook property.
rubric.description: States that ionic compounds are generally soluble in water.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for this property.

rubric.why: Mobile ions allow electrical conduction in molten or aqueous ionic compounds.
rubric.description: States that ionic compounds conduct electricity when molten or dissolved in water.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for this property; do not award for claiming they conduct as solids.

modelAnswer: Ionic compounds are generally hard crystalline solids with high melting and boiling points.
They are generally soluble in water.
They conduct electricity when molten or dissolved in water, but not in the solid state.

items.followUp: What is a polyatomic ion? Give one example.

rubric.why: A radical is identified as an atom or group of atoms carrying a charge and acting as a unit.
rubric.description: Defines a radical as an atom or group of atoms carrying a charge and behaving as a single unit.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the definition.

rubric.why: A charged ion is a suitable example of a radical.
rubric.description: Gives a correct example, such as sulfate, nitrate, ammonium, or carbonate.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for a correct example.

modelAnswer: A radical is an atom or group of atoms that carries a charge and behaves as a single unit in a chemical reaction.
For example, the sulfate radical is SO₄²⁻.

items.followUp: How many particles are present in 0.5 mole of oxygen molecules?

rubric.why: Avogadro’s number is the number of particles in one mole.
rubric.description: States Avogadro’s number as approximately 6.02 × 10²³ particles per mole.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the correct value and meaning.

rubric.why: A correct example applies the number to a mole of a substance.
rubric.description: Gives an example, such as one mole of carbon containing approximately 6.02 × 10²³ carbon atoms.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for a suitable example with the correct particle count.

modelAnswer: Avogadro’s number is the number of particles present in one mole of a substance: 6.02 × 10²³ mol⁻¹.
For example, one mole of carbon contains 6.02 × 10²³ carbon atoms.

items.followUp: Describe two conclusions drawn from Rutherford’s alpha-particle scattering experiment.

rubric.why: This is the principal observation that most of the atom is empty space.
rubric.description: States that most alpha particles passed through the gold foil without deflection.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for this observation.

rubric.why: Deflection of a small number of alpha particles is another key observation.
rubric.description: States that a small number of alpha particles were deflected, with a very few rebounding or being deflected through large angles.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for this observation.

modelAnswer: Most alpha particles passed straight through the gold foil without being deflected.
A small number were deflected, and a very few bounced back or were deflected through large angles.
